learning_objective: 🎯 Master the strict, legal format of how companies must present their assets, liabilities, and profits according to Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Unlike partnership accounts (T-shape), company Balance Sheets are vertical. The top half shows 'Equity and Liabilities' (where the money came from), and the bottom half shows 'Assets' (where the money went).

Current assets/liabilities are short-term (expected to be converted to cash or paid within 12 months or the operating cycle). Non-Current means long-term (more than 12 months, like buildings or 5-year loans).
Tangible assets can be touched (Machinery, Land, Computers). Intangible assets have huge value but no physical form (Goodwill, Patents, Computer Software, Trademarks).
This replaces the old Trading and P&L account. It starts with 'Revenue from Operations' (Sales), adds 'Other Income', and then subtracts all specific Expenses to find 'Profit Before Tax'.

fun_activity.title: 🪣 The 12-Month Sorting Bucket
fun_activity.instructions: Take a piece of paper and draw a line down the middle. Label the left 'Current' and right 'Non-Current'. Now quickly sort these items: A 5-year bank loan, Cash in wallet, A delivery truck, Unsold inventory. Did you put Cash and Inventory in the 'Current' bucket?

exam_tips: 📌 Memorizing the major headings and sub-headings of the Balance Sheet is non-negotiable. 3-4 marks are guaranteed just for stating the correct Head and Sub-head of an item (e.g., 'Loose Tools' -> Head: Current Assets, Sub-head: Inventories).
📌 'Proposed Dividend' is shown as a Contingent Liability in the Notes to Accounts, NOT inside the main Balance Sheet.
📌 'Revenue from Operations' for a financial company means Interest and Dividend received, but for a non-financial company, it means Sales.
quick_recap: ⭐ Companies must strictly follow Part I (Balance Sheet) and Part II (Statement of P&L) of Schedule III.
⭐ The Operating Cycle is the time between buying raw materials and getting cash from selling the final product.
⭐ Contingent liabilities are 'possible' future liabilities (like a pending court case) shown in footnotes.
